analysis.one_liner: Imposes a new federal tax on big investors buying single-family homes.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 9 Democratic cosponsors, has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since its January 2026 referral with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill puts a tax on corporations and other large investors each time they buy an existing single-family home: 1% for investors owning 16 to 25 homes, 3% for those owning 26 to 100, and 5% for those owning more than 100. It does not touch people buying their own home, or nonprofits and governments building affordable housing. The money raised — 65% — would go to the federal Housing Trust Fund and 35% to the Capital Magnet Fund, which finance affordable housing. The bill has been referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has seen no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: First-time and ordinary homebuyers who compete against deep-pocketed investors at the closing table, and renters in markets where corporate landlords have bought up housing stock. The tax raises the cost to large investors of outbidding families for existing homes, and its revenue funds affordable housing construction.

how_it_helps.text: The tax applies only to investors — 1% of purchase price for investors owning 16-25 homes, 3% for 26-100, and 5% for more than 100 — and never to individuals buying a principal residence.
The bill aggregates related companies as a single investor, so splitting a portfolio across LLCs does not dodge the tax, and it taxes purchases made through related parties.

65% of the revenue goes to the Housing Trust Fund and 35% to the Capital Magnet Fund, which finance affordable housing, with an exception for nonprofits, states, public housing authorities, land banks, and community land trusts.
New construction is excluded from the tax, steering investors toward adding housing supply rather than buying up existing homes.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate and large-scale investors who buy existing single-family homes, including REITs, private equity firms, and single-family rental companies. To the extent the tax discourages their purchases, they also lose acquisitions; some of the tax could be passed to renters through higher rents if investors still buy.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate landlords and big home investors

drawbacks.text: The tax also reaches mid-sized investors owning just 16 homes, which could include smaller local landlords, and if investors keep buying, the cost may be passed through to renters in higher rents.

In markets where large investors supply rental housing, discouraging their purchases does not add homes to the for-sale market on its own — the revenue-to-Housing-Trust-Fund mechanism, not the tax, is what builds anything.
The tax is modest relative to home prices (1-5%), so it may raise costs for investors without meaningfully changing who wins home purchases in hot markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to buyers is real but modest — a 1-5% purchase tax is a speed bump, not a wall, for investors who outbid families with cash. The stronger part is the dedicated revenue stream for affordable housing. The main risk is that costs are passed to renters rather than changing investor behavior.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any floor action since late January 2026.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the bill on January 30, 2026, with nine Democratic cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The Senate Finance Committee has taken no further action on the bill — no markup, no hearing, no committee vote — and it has never reached the Senate floor.
All nine cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Senate Finance Committee is chaired by a Republican in a chamber Republicans control with 55 seats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, institutional buyers of single-family homes: no tax has been enacted, and they continue purchasing homes without the new 1-5% levy while the bill waits in committee.

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental investors and corporate landlords
industries.note: The bill taxes every existing home they buy at 1-5% of the purchase price, directly raising their cost of acquiring the homes that families bid on. These investors profit by outbidding ordinary buyers and converting owner-occupied homes to rentals.

industries.industry: Private equity and REITs with housing portfolios
industries.note: Aggregation rules treat related companies and family holdings as one investor, closing the common structure-splitting route around ownership thresholds. Their model of assembling large scattered-site home portfolios gets more expensive.

Newly built homes are excluded from the tax, tilting investor capital toward construction rather than buying up existing homes. This adds supply instead of just reshuffling ownership of the same houses.

industries.industry: Affordable housing nonprofits, land banks, and community land trusts
industries.note: They are exempt from the tax and are the intended beneficiaries of its revenue — 65% to the Housing Trust Fund and 35% to the Capital Magnet Fund — which finance affordable housing they build and manage.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor, all-Democratic cosponsors, and has sat untouched in the Republican-chaired Finance Committee since January 2026. Absent Republican support or a leadership decision to prioritize it, the most likely path is that it dies in committee at the end of this Congress, as most first-term housing tax bills do.
